findings.what: The right answer is always the first button (1500 rpm, 200 V, the regenerating fan), so by screen 4 he can answer by position; move the right answer to the second or third place on at least two of the checks.

findings.where: Screens 2-3 (How it works, Volts per hertz)
findings.what: No screen says why flux follows volts per hertz: the half-cycle reason and the transformer link are only in explain and analogy, and a steps lesson never shows those, so add one or two sentences on screen 3, for example 'The stator is a winding on iron, like a transformer. Its flux goes with volts per hertz.', in place of the repeated UNDER sentences.

findings.where: Screen 7 (Faults and tests), Safety first row and the matching Keep this trap
findings.what: The safe-isolation steps only prove the DC bus dead: they never say to prove the tester, or to prove the input and motor terminals dead, and they skip the researched warning that a cabinet-door isolator may not kill the input busbars; that content is in practice.text, which a steps lesson never shows.

The screen runs to 106 words across six cards, over the 90-word limit; trim it, for example by dropping 'Charged, the bus holds about 540 V DC' (screen 2 already gives it) and shortening the Overcurrent row, while making room for the proving-dead line above.

findings.where: Screen 6 (Where it is used, and its limits)
findings.what: The screen runs to 97 words plus the chart labels, over 90; cut the Savings row (the chart already shows 42% and 12.5%), and replace the unclear 'Treat them as the ideal' with 'Real systems save less.'

findings.where: Screen 5 (How it behaves), Above base speed row
findings.what: 'The power stays about constant, so the torque falls as it speeds up' reads as the power actually drawn, but it is the power and torque the motor can give; on a fan the load power keeps rising above base speed. Say 'The power it can give stays about constant, so the torque it can give falls', which is how the Keep this trap already puts it.

The read starts at 60 Hz and then says 'Held at 400 V instead, 40 Hz would give 10 V per hertz' before the normal 40 Hz case it is 'instead' of, so a tired reader has to read it twice; put it back in the order of the verified JSON (falls with frequency, then held, then above 50 Hz), split the 20-word 'At 60 Hz it still gives 400 V, the field turns...' sentence, and get it under about 90 words.

findings.where: Screen 3 (Volts per hertz), words under the picture
findings.what: The task, the live line, the UNDER paragraph, the example note and the Hold 400 V hint come to about 100-110 words; the UNDER paragraph repeats what the live line already says as he drags ('Above it, the volts stop at 400 V and the flux falls'), so keep its first sentence (base speed, in amber) and give the room to the flux-follows-V/f sentence.

The right option is twice as long as the others and is the only one that names a mechanism, which gives it away; give the wrong options the same shape, for example 'The fan is overloaded and the motor draws too much current' and 'The supply has lost a phase and the bus sags'.

findings.where: Screen 1 (Do you still have it?), the 750 rpm hint
findings.what: 'That form counts pole pairs, not poles' leaves 'that form' vague; say it outright: '60 × f ÷ p works with pole pairs: 60 × 50 ÷ 2 = 1500 rpm.'

findings.where: Screen 4 (Check on the cause), the 100 V hint
findings.what: 'It falls in step with the frequency only once' is cryptic; say 'Halve the frequency and the voltage halves once: 8 × 25 = 200 V.'

findings.where: Keep this card, the rule lines and traps
findings.what: 'Isolate and wait the drive's discharge time' should read 'wait out' or 'wait for', and the card's 'Common trips' line names undervoltage and over temperature, which no screen explains; either give each a few words or keep the list to the trips the lesson teaches.

findings.where: Screen 5 or the Keep this card (marine line)
findings.what: There is no line for a ship's supply, though the brief (question 5) asked for one and research holds the RN's 440 V, 60 Hz: add one computed line, '440 ÷ 60 = 7.33 V per Hz, and base speed is 60 Hz on a ship's motor', so he does not carry 50 Hz as the base everywhere.

findings.where: Screen 5 or the Keep this card (practice points)
findings.what: practice.text's 'Check the motor and the load can run safely over the whole speed range' (sourced) never reaches a screen; one line would cover it, with the cube law already shown: a fan at 60 Hz needs 1.2³ = 1.73 times its 50 Hz power.
